title: A Chemogenetic CRISPR Knock-out Screen Uncovers Synergy Between Ubiquitin Signaling and C16orf72/HAPSTR1 for S-phase Entry
projectDescription: Cell cycle progression is orchestrated by complex interplay between post-translational modifications (PTMs) controlling activation (phosphorylation) and degradation (ubiquitination) of key cell cycle regulators. To comprehensively identify ubiquitin signalling components critical for cell proliferation, we employed a chemical-genetic CRISPR knock-out screen exploiting the first-in-class ubiquitin E1 inhibitor TAK243. We identified 239 genes, including C16orf72/HAPSTR1, whose mutation rendered cells sensitive and 55 genes conferring resistance to diminished ubiquitin signaling, providing a systems view of key protein networks underpinning cell cycle progression. Proteome-wide alterations in the ubiquitin signaling landscape as a function of HAPSTR1 expression, revealed increased ubiquitination of the cell cycle regulator CDK6. Mechanistically, we find that HAPSTR1 controls the timing of S-phase entry via RB-E2F1 pathway activation by CDK6. Strikingly, the HAPSTR1/CDK6 axis is finetuned by the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), enforcing cell cycle-dependent turnover of both proteins. Although CDKs have long been thought of as stable elements of the cell cycle machinery, this conventional notion is challenged by our present findings, demonstrating UPS-dependent fluctuations in CDK6 expression. Altogether, we provide a valuable resource on the interplay between the ubiquitin system and cell proliferation and uncover HAPSTR1 as a regulator of CDK6 levels to orchestrate G1/S transition.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Enrichment and mass spectrometry of endogenous ubiquitin substrates in RPE1 p53-/- TetOn cas9 (5 replicates) and HAPSTR1 KO.2 (5 replicates) cells using UbiSite was performed as previously described 43, PMID: 36408944, PMID: 35585066. In brief, cells were treated with MG132, washed twice with ice-cold PBS, scraped, and lysed in lysis buffer (Guanidine Hydrochloride 8 M in 50 mM HEPES solution, pH 8.5). After sonication for 30 seconds lysates were centrifuged at 16000 RCF for 15 minutes and protein concentration of each condition’s replica was measures with BCA Kit (Thermo Scientific Pierce, PI23227). Proteins were subjected to reduction with DTT (2 mM, 30 min at room temperature), alkylation with Chloroacetamide (11 mM, 30 min at room temperature in the dark) and digestion with LysC enzyme (WAKO) overnight (enzyme:protein ratio was 1:100). Peptides mixture was purified using C18 cartridge (Waters, WAT051910) and lyophilized for 24 hours. The LysC digested peptides were dissolved in ice-cold IAP buffer ( 50 mm MOPS–NaOH (pH 7.6), 10 mm Na2HPO4, 50 mm NaCl) in presence of 0.1 % Triton X100. After brief centrifugation (16000 RCF, 5 minutes) peptides concentration was measured with a Nanodrop (Implen, NanoPhotomiter). Three mg of peptides from each replica were mixed with 30 µl of UbiSite antibody-agarose beads 50 % slurry (the UbiSite antibody was bound and cross-linked to agarose beads as described earlier (PMID: 29967540)) and incubated for 4 hours at 4 °C slowly rotating (10 RPM). After incubation the beads were washed with 1 ml of ice-cold IAP buffer and captured peptides were eluted 3 times with 0.1 % TFA. The eluted peptides were further neutralized with HEPES buffer (100 mM, pH 8.0) and digested with 100 ng of Trypsin at 37 °C for 12 hours.  Mass spectrometry acquisition The complex mixtures of peptides were purified using Stage Tips (PMID: 17703201), spiked with iRT standard peptides (Biognosys AG, Switzerland) and subjected to nanoLC-MS/MS analysis using an EASY-nLC 1000 ultra-high-pressure system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) connected online with the Orbitrap Exploris 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides mix from each replica was loaded into a fused silica column home-packed with 1.9 µm Reprosil C18 beads (Dr-Maisch, r119.b9.) in solvent A (0.5 % acetic acid). Peptides were eluted with a gradient of solvent B (80 % Acetonitrile, 0.5 % acetic acid) from 5 % to 95 % at flow rate of 250 nL/min. Data was acquired for 120 minutes using DIA method with the following settings: mass range 350-1400 m/z, profile data type, normalized AGC target of 300% with 120,000 resolution and 45 ms of maximum injection time for MS1 scans. DIA setup for 56 windows with 12 Da and overlap of 1 Da was used. Precursor Mass range was 361 – 1033 m/z. Acquired scans had normalized AGC target value set at 1000%, Orbitrap resolution was 30,000 and maximum Injection time 54 ms. The collision energy was set at 28%.
dataProcessingProtocol: Data analysis Raw mass spectrometry files were analyzed using Spectronaut (version 18.1.230626.50606) using Direct DIA approach and “Pulsar” search engine with the following parameters: Enzymes for protein digestion was Trypsin with 2 missed cleavages and exclusion for cleavage before Proline, minimum peptide length was 7 residues. PSM, Peptide and Protein Group FDRs were set to 0.01, PTM Localization Filter was active with minimum Localization Threshold set to 0.75. We used a UniProt database (Reviewed SwissProt from October 2019 of Homo Sapiens) with 20,351 entries for the Pulsar’s search. Acetyl (Protein N-term), Oxidation (M) and Ubiquitination (diGly on K) were set as variable peptides modifications, whereas Carbamidomethyl (C) was set as fixed peptide modification. Cross-Run Normalization was set as True with automatic Row Selection and Normalization Strategy.   The Spectronaut PTMs output table was filtered in Perseus (v2.0.7.0). Data were log2 transformed and filtered for identification in at least four out of five replicates of RPE1-p53-/- or HAPSTR1 KO.2. Missing values were imputed from the lower end of the normal distribution (default settings). A two-sided student’s t test with permutation-based FDR cells at 0.05 FDR (q value) and S0 = 0.1 was used for statistical analysis
